assessment.name: Year 10 Autumn Science Assessment (Biology part)
assessment.sections: Thursday 3 December, period 2. Section A: 45 multiple choice questions online across biology, chemistry and physics. Section B: written answers.
assessment.weighting: 60% this term's unit B4.1 The Digestive System. 40% Year 9 units: cells, genetics, biodiversity and human impact. Later units are set as not studied yet.
assessment.equipment: Chromebook, black pen, pencil, ruler, calculator

mock.note: 15 biology questions weighted 60/40. Do the chemistry and physics mocks too for the full 45.

group_labels.T: This term: B4.1 The digestive system (60%)
group_labels.L: Not in this assessment (marked not studied yet)

cards.title: Levels of organisation
cards.question: What are tissues, organs and organ systems, and how is the stomach an example?
points: Cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism.
A tissue is a group of similar cells with a similar structure and function.
An organ is a group of different tissues working together to do a specific job.
Stomach: muscular tissue churns, glandular tissue makes enzymes and acid, epithelial tissue lines it.
cards.watch_out: The stomach is an organ, not a tissue.
cards.grade9: Define fully: a tissue is a group of cells with a similar structure and function. Then use the stomach or leaf as a named example.

cards.title: Digestive enzymes
cards.question: Which enzymes digest carbohydrates, proteins and lipids, where are they made, and what are the products?
points: Carbohydrases (amylase): starch → sugars. Made in salivary glands, pancreas, small intestine.
Proteases: protein → amino acids. Made in the stomach, pancreas, small intestine.
Lipases: lipids → fatty acids and glycerol. Made in the pancreas and small intestine.
The products are absorbed and used to build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins. Some glucose is used in respiration.
cards.watch_out: Lipase gives two products, fatty acids and glycerol.
cards.grade9: Explain why digestion is needed. Large insoluble molecules must be broken into small soluble ones to be absorbed into the blood.

cards.title: How enzymes work
cards.question: How do enzymes work, and how do temperature and pH affect them?
points: Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts.
The substrate fits the active site: the lock and key model. Each enzyme is specific to one substrate.
Rate rises with temperature up to an optimum, about 37 °C for human enzymes.
Above the optimum, or far from the optimum pH, the active site changes shape and the enzyme is denatured.
cards.watch_out: Enzymes are denatured, not killed. Cold slows them but does not denature them.
cards.grade9: Say the substrate no longer fits the active site, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form. Collision language earns higher marks.

cards.title: The amylase and pH practical
cards.question: How do you find the effect of pH on the rate of amylase activity?
points: Mix amylase, starch and a buffer of one pH in a water bath at a fixed temperature.
Every 10 seconds, add a drop to iodine on a spotting tile.
When iodine stays orange-brown, all the starch has gone. Record the time.
Repeat at other pH values. The shortest time shows the optimum pH.
cards.watch_out: Blue-black means starch is still present.
cards.grade9: Name the control variables (temperature, volume and concentration of amylase and starch) and say why sampling every 10 s limits precision.

cards.title: Food tests
cards.question: How do you test for starch, sugars, protein and lipids?
points: Starch: iodine turns orange-brown to blue-black.
Reducing sugars: Benedict's, heat in a water bath. Blue to green, yellow, orange or brick red.
Protein: biuret reagent turns blue to purple.
Lipids: Sudan III stain gives a red-stained oily layer on top.
cards.watch_out: Benedict's is the only test that needs heating.
cards.grade9: Mention a safety point (eye protection, no naked flame near ethanol if used) and that Benedict's colour gives a rough idea of concentration.

cards.title: Bile
cards.question: What does bile do, and why is it not an enzyme?
points: Bile is made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder and released into the small intestine.
It is alkaline, so it neutralises stomach acid, giving the best pH for enzymes in the small intestine.
It emulsifies fats into small droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase.
cards.watch_out: Bile is not an enzyme. It breaks no chemical bonds.
cards.grade9: Link emulsification to faster digestion because of a larger surface area for lipase to act on.

cards.title: The digestive system and absorption
cards.question: What does each organ of the digestive system do, and how is the small intestine adapted for absorption?
points: Mouth: teeth break food up, salivary glands release amylase. Oesophagus: carries food to the stomach.
Stomach: churns food, makes protease and hydrochloric acid (kills bacteria, gives the right pH for stomach protease).
Liver makes bile; gall bladder stores it. Pancreas makes amylase, protease and lipase.
Small intestine: digestion finishes and soluble products are absorbed into the blood. Large intestine: absorbs water.
Villi give a huge surface area, have a single layer of surface cells and a good blood supply.
cards.watch_out: Bile is made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder, and is not an enzyme.
cards.hook: Mouth, Oesophagus, Stomach, Small intestine, Large intestine: My Old Shoes Smell Lovely.
cards.grade9: Link each villus feature to faster absorption by diffusion and active transport.

cards.title: Eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells
cards.question: How is a bacterial cell different from an animal or plant cell, and how big are they?
points: Eukaryotic cells (animal and plant) have DNA inside a nucleus. Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) do not.
Bacterial DNA is a single loop in the cytoplasm, often with small extra rings called plasmids.
Bacteria have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and a cell wall (not made of cellulose).
Prokaryotic cells are much smaller, roughly 1 to 10 µm, compared with 10 to 100 µm for eukaryotic cells.
cards.watch_out: Never draw a bacterium with a nucleus or mitochondria.
cards.grade9: Use orders of magnitude to compare. A 100 µm plant cell is 10² times bigger than a 1 µm bacterium. Show it as a power of ten.

cards.title: Parts of animal and plant cells
cards.question: What does each part of an animal cell do, and what extra parts does a plant cell have?
points: Nucleus: holds the genetic material and controls the cell. Cytoplasm: where most chemical reactions happen.
Cell membrane: controls what goes in and out. Mitochondria: aerobic respiration. Ribosomes: protein synthesis.
Plant cells also have a cellulose cell wall (strengthens), chloroplasts (photosynthesis) and a permanent vacuole filled with cell sap.
cards.watch_out: Plant cells have mitochondria too. They respire all the time, day and night.
cards.grade9: Link structure to function in one sentence, for example many mitochondria means more aerobic respiration, so more energy for muscle contraction.

cards.title: Specialised cells and differentiation
cards.question: How are sperm, nerve, muscle, root hair, xylem and phloem cells adapted, and what is differentiation?
points: Sperm: tail, many mitochondria, acrosome with enzymes. Nerve: long with branched endings. Muscle: many mitochondria, protein fibres that contract.
Root hair: large surface area for water and mineral ions. Xylem: hollow dead cells strengthened by lignin. Phloem: sieve plates with companion cells.
Differentiation is a cell becoming specialised by gaining the sub-cellular structures for its job.
Most animal cells differentiate early. Many plant cells keep the ability to differentiate all their life.
cards.watch_out: Differentiation is a cell becoming specialised, not the cell dividing.
cards.grade9: When asked to explain an adaptation, always give feature, then function, then the benefit to the organism.

cards.title: Microscopes and magnification
cards.question: Why can an electron microscope show more than a light microscope, and how do you calculate magnification?
points: Electron microscopes have much higher magnification and resolution, so they show ribosomes and the inside of mitochondria.
Resolution is the ability to tell apart two points that are close together.
magnification = image size ÷ real size
Units: 1 mm = 1000 µm, 1 µm = 1000 nm.
cards.watch_out: Convert to the same unit before you divide. 12 ÷ 20 = 0.6 cannot be a microscope magnification.
cards.grade9: Give answers in standard form when asked, for example 0.000 02 m = 2 × 10⁻⁵ m. Rearranging the equation is a common higher tier mark.

cards.title: Chromosomes and mitosis
cards.question: What happens in the cell cycle, and why is mitosis needed?
points: Chromosomes are in the nucleus and are made of DNA. Body cells have chromosomes in pairs (23 pairs in humans).
Stage 1: the cell grows, copies its DNA and makes more ribosomes and mitochondria.
Stage 2, mitosis: one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell.
Stage 3: the cytoplasm and cell membrane divide to form two identical cells.
Mitosis is for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.
cards.watch_out: Mitosis makes two genetically identical cells with the full set. Meiosis makes four different gametes with half.
cards.grade9: Use precise language. Write genetically identical daughter cells, not the same cells.

cards.title: Stem cells and therapeutic cloning
cards.question: What are stem cells, where are they found, and what are the benefits and problems of using them?
points: A stem cell is undifferentiated. It can divide and become many types of cell.
Embryonic stem cells can become most cell types. Adult stem cells (bone marrow) form only some, such as blood cells. Plant meristems can form any plant cell.
Stem cells could treat diabetes and paralysis. Meristems are used to clone rare plants and crop plants quickly.
Therapeutic cloning: an embryo is made with the patient's own genes, so its stem cells are not rejected.
Concerns: ethical and religious objections to using embryos, and the risk of passing on a viral infection.
cards.watch_out: Therapeutic cloning avoids rejection because the cells have the same genes as the patient.
cards.grade9: Evaluate questions need benefits, risks and a justified conclusion. End with a sentence that weighs them, for example the benefits outweigh the risks if...

cards.title: Diffusion
cards.question: What is diffusion, and what affects its rate?
points: Diffusion is the spreading out of particles, resulting in net movement from higher to lower concentration.
It is passive. It needs no energy from respiration.
Examples: oxygen and carbon dioxide in gas exchange, urea from cells into the blood plasma.
Faster with a steeper concentration gradient, a higher temperature and a larger surface area.
cards.watch_out: Say net movement. Particles still move both ways.
cards.grade9: Use the phrase down a concentration gradient and name where the particles move from and to.

cards.title: Osmosis and the potato practical
cards.question: What is osmosis, and how do you find the concentration of potato cell sap?
points: Osmosis is the diffusion of water from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane.
Required practical: weigh potato cylinders, leave in different sugar or salt solutions, dry and reweigh.
% change in mass = (final mass − initial mass) ÷ initial mass × 100
Plot % change against concentration. Where the line crosses zero, there is no net movement of water.
cards.watch_out: Blot cylinders dry before weighing, or surface water adds false mass.
cards.grade9: Explain loss of mass as water moving out by osmosis because the solution outside is more concentrated than the cell sap.

cards.title: Active transport
cards.question: What is active transport, and where does it happen?
points: Active transport moves substances from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated one, against the concentration gradient.
It needs energy from respiration.
Root hair cells take in mineral ions this way from very dilute soil water.
Glucose is absorbed from the small intestine into the blood by active transport, even when blood sugar is higher.
cards.watch_out: Mineral ions enter roots by active transport, not diffusion or osmosis.
cards.grade9: Link active transport to many mitochondria in the cell. That link often earns the last mark.

cards.title: Surface area to volume ratio and exchange surfaces
cards.question: Why do large organisms need exchange surfaces, and how are they adapted?
points: As an organism gets bigger, its surface area to volume ratio gets smaller.
Diffusion across the outer surface alone is too slow for large organisms.
Exchange surfaces have a large surface area, thin membranes for a short diffusion path, and (in animals) a good blood supply and ventilation.
Examples: alveoli, villi in the small intestine, fish gill filaments, root hairs, leaves.
cards.watch_out: A bigger cube has a smaller ratio. A 4 cm cube is 96 : 64 = 1.5 : 1.
cards.grade9: Explain each adaptation by how it increases rate of diffusion, for example good blood supply keeps the concentration gradient steep.

cards.title: Culturing microorganisms (biology only)
cards.question: How do bacteria multiply, and how do you grow an uncontaminated culture?
points: Bacteria multiply by binary fission. In good conditions some divide every 20 minutes.
Number of bacteria = starting number × 2ⁿ, where n is the number of divisions.
Aseptic technique: sterilise Petri dishes and agar, pass the inoculating loop through a flame, tape the lid on (not fully sealed) and store it upside down.
Incubate at 25 °C in schools, which slows the growth of human pathogens.

example.heading: Required practical, antibiotics
lines: Clear zone radius 6 mm, area = πr² = 3.14 × 6² = 113 mm²
The bigger the clear zone, the more effective the antibiotic

cards.watch_out: Taping the lid fully shut would stop oxygen getting in and encourage harmful anaerobic bacteria.
cards.grade9: In time questions, divide total time by division time first to find n, then work out 2ⁿ. State the answer in standard form if it is large.

cards.title: Cancer
cards.question: What is cancer, and what is the difference between benign and malignant tumours?
points: Cancer is the result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division by mitosis.
Benign tumours grow in one area, usually inside a membrane, and do not invade other parts of the body.
Malignant tumours invade neighbouring tissues and spread to other parts of the body in the blood, forming secondary tumours.
Risk factors: lifestyle (smoking, obesity, UV exposure) and genetic factors.
cards.watch_out: Benign tumours can still be dangerous if they press on organs such as the brain.
cards.hook: Benign = Be nice (stays put). Malignant = Moves (spreads).
cards.grade9: Link cancer to a failure in control of the cell cycle and mitosis.

cards.title: Sexual and asexual reproduction
cards.question: How do sexual and asexual reproduction differ, and what are the advantages of each?
points: Sexual: two parents, gametes made by meiosis fuse, offspring vary. Asexual: one parent, mitosis, clones.
Advantages of sexual: variation, so a species can survive environmental change; natural selection; selective breeding.
Advantages of asexual: one parent needed, faster, uses less energy, many identical offspring when conditions are good.
Some organisms do both: malaria parasites, fungi (spores), strawberries (runners and seeds), daffodils (bulbs and seeds).
cards.watch_out: Asexual reproduction uses mitosis. No gametes are made.
cards.grade9: In compare questions write a matching point for each method in the same sentence, using whereas.

cards.title: Meiosis
cards.question: What happens in meiosis, and why is it important?
points: Meiosis happens in the testes and ovaries to make gametes.
The chromosomes are copied, then the cell divides twice to make four gametes.
Each gamete has a single set of chromosomes and is genetically different.
At fertilisation, gametes join to restore the full number. The new cell then divides by mitosis.
cards.watch_out: Meiosis makes four different cells with half the chromosomes.
cards.grade9: Explain that meiosis produces variation, which is the raw material for natural selection.

cards.title: DNA and the genome
cards.question: How are DNA, chromosomes, genes and the genome related?
points: DNA is a polymer of two strands in a double helix, coiled into chromosomes in the nucleus.
A gene is a small section of DNA that codes for a sequence of amino acids to make a specific protein.
The genome is the entire genetic material of an organism.
Studying the human genome helps find genes linked to disease, treat inherited disorders and trace human migration.
cards.watch_out: A chromosome carries many genes.
cards.grade9: Use the hierarchy in order, genome → chromosome → gene → base sequence, to show precise understanding.

cards.title: DNA structure and protein synthesis (biology only)
cards.question: What is DNA made of, and how is a protein made from a gene?
points: DNA is made of repeating nucleotides. Each has a sugar, a phosphate group and one of four bases (A, C, G, T).
Complementary base pairs: A with T, C with G.
A sequence of three bases codes for one amino acid.
Higher: a copy of the gene is made and moves to the ribosome; carrier molecules bring amino acids in the right order; the chain folds into a specific shape.
Mutations change the base sequence. Most have no effect; some change the protein's shape, for example an enzyme's active site.
cards.watch_out: Non-coding DNA can still switch genes on and off.
cards.grade9: Link a mutation to the chain of effects, changed base sequence, changed amino acid order, changed protein shape, changed function.

cards.title: Alleles and genetic terms
cards.question: What do allele, dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, genotype and phenotype mean?
points: Alleles are different versions of the same gene. You inherit one from each parent.
Dominant (B) shows with one copy. Recessive (b) shows only with two (bb).
Homozygous: two identical alleles (BB or bb). Heterozygous: two different alleles (Bb).
Genotype is the alleles present (Bb). Phenotype is the characteristic shown (brown eyes).
Most characteristics are controlled by several genes interacting.
cards.watch_out: BB and Bb have the same phenotype but different genotypes.
cards.grade9: Always define your symbols with a key before drawing a Punnett square.

cards.title: Punnett squares and inherited disorders
cards.question: How do you predict offspring, and how are cystic fibrosis and polydactyly inherited?
points: Put one parent's alleles across the top and the other's down the side. Each box is a 1 in 4 chance.
Cystic fibrosis: recessive allele (f), a disorder of cell membranes. Ff people are carriers.
Polydactyly (extra digits): dominant allele (D), so one copy is enough.
Embryo screening and possible gene therapy raise ethical, social and economic issues.

example.heading: Ff × Ff
lines: Chance of cystic fibrosis = 1 in 4 = 25%; ratio unaffected : affected = 3 : 1

cards.watch_out: The probability applies to each child separately.
cards.grade9: Give probability in the form asked (fraction, percentage, ratio) and do not mix them up. 3 : 1 is not 1 in 3.

cards.title: Sex determination
cards.question: How is sex inherited?
points: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes. One pair are the sex chromosomes.
Females are XX and males are XY.
Every egg carries an X. Half of sperm carry X and half carry Y.
The chance of a boy or girl is 50% each time.
cards.watch_out: The sperm decides the sex, not the egg.
cards.grade9: Draw a genetic diagram with gametes shown in circles. It earns method marks even if the final answer slips.

cards.title: Biodiversity
cards.question: What is biodiversity, and why is it important?
points: Biodiversity is the variety of all the different species of organisms on Earth, or within an ecosystem.
High biodiversity makes an ecosystem more stable because species depend less on any one other species for food, shelter and the environment.
The future of the human species may depend on maintaining biodiversity.
Many human activities reduce biodiversity; only recently have measures been taken to stop this.
cards.watch_out: Biodiversity is about the number of different species, not the number of individuals.
cards.grade9: Explain stability with an example, such as a predator with many prey species surviving the loss of one.

cards.title: Waste management and pollution
cards.question: How do more people and more waste affect land, water and air?
points: The human population is growing rapidly and the standard of living is rising, so more resources are used and more waste is produced.
Water: sewage, fertiliser and toxic chemicals pollute water.
Air: smoke and acidic gases pollute the air.
Land: landfill and toxic chemicals such as pesticides and herbicides pollute land and may wash into water.
Pollution kills plants and animals, reducing biodiversity.
cards.watch_out: Name the pollutant and where it ends up, for example fertiliser runs off into rivers.
cards.grade9: Use chains of cause and effect, more people, more waste, pollution, loss of species, lower biodiversity.

cards.title: Land use and peat bogs
cards.question: How do humans reduce the land available for other animals and plants, and why is destroying peat bogs a problem?
points: Humans use land for building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste, reducing habitats.
Peat bogs are destroyed to produce cheap garden compost.
This reduces the area of the habitat and the variety of species living there.
Peat decays or is burned, releasing carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
cards.watch_out: Peat is a store of carbon. Using it adds CO₂ to the air.
cards.grade9: Evaluate peat-free compost, protects habitats and carbon stores, but can cost more.

cards.title: Deforestation
cards.question: Why are tropical forests cut down, and what are the effects?
points: Large-scale deforestation in tropical areas provides land for cattle and rice fields, and grows crops for biofuels.
Fewer trees means less carbon dioxide is removed from the air by photosynthesis.
Burning or decay of the wood releases carbon dioxide.
Habitats are destroyed, reducing biodiversity.
cards.watch_out: Deforestation increases CO₂ in two ways, less absorbed and more released.
cards.hook: Cows, Rice, Fuel: the three reasons for tropical deforestation.
cards.grade9: Link deforestation to both global warming and loss of biodiversity in one answer.

cards.title: Global warming
cards.question: What causes global warming, and what are its biological consequences?
points: Levels of carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere are increasing, contributing to global warming.
Consequences: loss of habitat as sea levels rise and land floods.
Changes in the distribution of species as temperature and rainfall change.
Changes to the migration patterns of animals, and reduced biodiversity.
cards.watch_out: Give biological consequences in biology papers, not just melting ice.
cards.grade9: Explain why species distribution changes, some species can survive in new areas while others lose their habitat.

cards.title: Maintaining biodiversity
cards.question: What can be done to reduce the negative effects of humans on ecosystems and biodiversity?
points: Breeding programmes for endangered species.
Protection and regeneration of rare habitats.
Reintroduction of field margins and hedgerows where farmers grow only one crop.
Reduction of deforestation and carbon dioxide emissions by some governments.
Recycling resources rather than dumping waste in landfill.
cards.watch_out: Conflicts exist, for example protecting land can cost farmers money or food production.
cards.grade9: Discuss conflicting pressures, cost, food security, employment, and give a balanced judgement.

cards.title: Equations and calculations
cards.question: Can you write each equation and its units from memory?
points: magnification = image size ÷ real size
% change in mass = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100
rate = 1 ÷ time (enzyme practical); area of clear zone = πr²
bacteria after n divisions = start × 2ⁿ
rate of flow or transpiration = amount ÷ time
cards.watch_out: Convert units first, show working, and give an appropriate number of significant figures.
cards.grade9: Round only at the end and match the significant figures in the data.

cards.title: Required practicals in these topics
cards.question: Can you describe the method, variables and results for each practical?
points: RP1 Microscopy: prepare a slide, stain, focus from low to high power, draw and calculate magnification.
RP2 Antibiotics (biology only): aseptic technique, measure clear zones, πr².
RP3 Osmosis: potato cylinders in sugar or salt solutions, % change in mass.
RP4 Food tests: iodine, Benedict's, biuret, Sudan III.
RP5 Enzymes: amylase and starch at different pH, timed with iodine.
cards.watch_out: Name independent, dependent and control variables in every practical answer.
cards.grade9: Suggest a specific improvement, for example use a colorimeter instead of judging colour by eye.

cards.title: The heart and circulation
cards.question: How does blood flow through the heart, and how is the heart rate controlled?
points: The heart is a double pump. The right side pumps blood to the lungs, the left side pumps it round the body.
Body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta.
Valves stop backflow. The left ventricle wall is thicker to pump blood at higher pressure.
Pacemaker cells in the right atrium control the natural resting heart rate. An artificial pacemaker corrects irregular rhythms.
Coronary arteries supply the heart muscle with oxygenated blood.
cards.watch_out: Diagrams face you, so the heart's left side is on your right.
cards.grade9: Explain why a double circulation is efficient. Blood returns to the heart after the lungs so it can be pumped round the body at high pressure.

cards.title: Blood vessels and blood
cards.question: How are arteries, veins and capillaries adapted, and what are the parts of blood?
points: Arteries: thick muscular and elastic walls for high pressure. Veins: thin walls, wide lumen, valves. Capillaries: walls one cell thick for diffusion.
Plasma carries cells, glucose, CO₂, urea and hormones. Red cells: haemoglobin, no nucleus, biconcave shape.
White cells fight pathogens. Platelets are cell fragments that help clotting.
cards.watch_out: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood. Arteries are named by direction, away from the heart.
cards.grade9: Use the term lumen and explain that valves in veins are needed because pressure is low.

cards.title: The lungs
cards.question: How are the lungs adapted for gas exchange?
points: Air path: trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.
Alveoli give a huge surface area. Walls are one cell thick, as are the capillary walls.
A rich capillary network and breathing keep the concentration gradients steep.
Oxygen diffuses into the blood; carbon dioxide diffuses into the alveoli.
cards.watch_out: Gas exchange is diffusion, not active transport.
cards.grade9: Name all three factors of a good exchange surface and link each to faster diffusion.

cards.title: Coronary heart disease and treatments
cards.question: What causes coronary heart disease, and what are the pros and cons of each treatment?
points: Fatty material builds up in coronary arteries, narrowing them and reducing oxygen to the heart muscle.
Stents keep arteries open. Quick recovery, but risk of blood clots.
Statins lower blood cholesterol. Taken long term, with possible side effects.
Faulty valves: mechanical (lasts long, needs anti-clotting drugs) or biological (from animals or donors).
Heart transplant or artificial heart while waiting. Donors are scarce and rejection is a risk.
cards.watch_out: Coronary arteries feed the heart muscle itself.
cards.grade9: Compare treatments using cost, recovery time, risk and how long the effect lasts.

cards.title: Health, risk factors and cancer
cards.question: What affects health, and what is the difference between benign and malignant tumours?
points: Health is a state of physical and mental wellbeing. Diseases can interact, for example a weak immune system raises infection risk.
Risk factors: smoking (lung disease, cancer), poor diet and inactivity (obesity, type 2 diabetes), alcohol (liver, brain), carcinogens and ionising radiation.
Benign tumours stay in one place, often in a membrane. Malignant tumours invade tissue and spread in the blood to form secondary tumours.
cards.watch_out: A correlation is not proof of cause. A mechanism is needed.
cards.grade9: When analysing data on risk factors, comment on sample size, correlation and whether a causal mechanism is known.

cards.title: Plant tissues and the leaf
cards.question: How is a leaf built as an organ, and what does each tissue do?
points: Epidermis: covers the leaf; a waxy cuticle reduces water loss.
Palisade mesophyll: many chloroplasts for photosynthesis. Spongy mesophyll: air spaces for gas diffusion.
Xylem and phloem transport. Meristem tissue at root and shoot tips makes new cells.
Guard cells open and close stomata to control gas exchange and water loss.
cards.watch_out: Stomata are holes. Guard cells are the cells around them.
cards.grade9: For each tissue, link structure to how it helps photosynthesis or reduces water loss.

cards.title: Transpiration and translocation
cards.question: What are transpiration and translocation, and what affects the rate of transpiration?
points: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from leaves, pulling a transpiration stream up the xylem.
Translocation is the movement of dissolved sugars through the phloem, up and down the plant.
Transpiration is faster when it is warmer, drier, windier and brighter.
A potometer measures water uptake as an estimate of transpiration.
cards.watch_out: Transpiration happens in xylem; translocation in phloem.
cards.grade9: Explain each factor with particles, for example wind removes water vapour, keeping the concentration gradient steep.

cards.title: Mendel and the history of genetics (biology only)
cards.question: What did Mendel discover, and why was his work not accepted at first?
points: In the mid 1800s Mendel bred pea plants and saw characteristics passed on in units that were not blended.
He found some characteristics were dominant and some recessive, and predicted ratios.
His work was ignored because chromosomes, genes and DNA were not yet known, and he was not a well-known scientist.
Late 1800s: chromosomes seen. Early 1900s: genes on chromosomes. 1950s: DNA structure found.
cards.watch_out: Mendel never used the word gene. He called them inherited factors.
cards.grade9: History of science answers score highly when you explain why ideas were accepted, more evidence and new technology.

cards.title: Variation and mutation
cards.question: What causes variation, and where do new alleles come from?
points: Variation is caused by genes, the environment, or both.
There is usually a lot of genetic variation in a population.
New alleles arise by mutation, a change in DNA. Mutations happen all the time.
Most have no effect. Rarely one gives a new phenotype suited to the environment, which can lead to rapid change.
cards.watch_out: Environmental variation, such as a scar, is not inherited.
cards.grade9: Use examples for each cause, eye colour (genes), scar (environment), height (both).

cards.title: Evolution by natural selection
cards.question: How does natural selection lead to evolution?
points: Individuals in a population show variation, some caused by mutation.
Those with characteristics best suited to the environment are more likely to survive and reproduce.
They pass on their alleles, so these become more common in later generations.
Over many generations the population changes. This is evolution.
Evolution is a change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time.
cards.watch_out: Organisms do not change because they need to. The variation exists first.
cards.grade9: A 6 mark natural selection answer needs, in order, variation, mutation, competition or pressure, survival, reproduction, alleles passed on, many generations.

cards.title: Darwin, Wallace and speciation (biology only)
cards.question: What did Darwin and Wallace contribute, and how do new species form?
points: Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, based on observations such as the Galapagos finches.
His ideas were resisted: religious objections, not enough evidence, and no knowledge of genes.
Wallace independently proposed natural selection and worked on warning colouration.
Speciation: populations become isolated (for example geographically), conditions differ, natural selection acts differently, until they can no longer interbreed to give fertile offspring.
cards.watch_out: A new species means they cannot produce fertile offspring together, not just that they look different.
cards.grade9: Name the type of isolation and stress that each population builds up different alleles over many generations.

cards.title: Selective breeding
cards.question: How is selective breeding done, and what are the risks?
points: Humans choose parents with a useful characteristic and breed them.
Offspring with the characteristic are bred again over many generations.
Uses: disease resistant crops, more meat or milk, gentle dogs, large or unusual flowers.
Inbreeding reduces variation, so some breeds are prone to disease or inherited defects.
cards.watch_out: In selective breeding people choose. In natural selection the environment does.
cards.grade9: Explain why low variation is a risk. A new disease could affect the whole population because none have resistance alleles.

cards.title: Genetic engineering
cards.question: What is genetic engineering, how is it done, and what are the concerns?
points: Genetic engineering changes an organism's genome by adding a gene from another organism.
Examples: bacteria making human insulin; GM crops resistant to insects or herbicides, or with bigger yields.
Higher: enzymes cut out the gene; it is inserted into a vector (plasmid or virus); the vector carries it into the cells, at an early stage of development.
Concerns: effects on wild plants and insects, long-term health effects not fully known. Gene therapy may treat inherited disorders.
cards.watch_out: The vector carries the gene; it is not the gene itself.
cards.grade9: Balance benefits against concerns with specific examples, then make a judgement.

cards.title: Cloning (biology only)
cards.question: What are the four main methods of cloning?
points: Tissue culture: small groups of plant cells grow into new plants, to preserve rare species or for nurseries.
Cuttings: gardeners grow new plants from cut stems.
Embryo transplants: split an early animal embryo, implant the parts into host mothers.
Adult cell cloning: remove the nucleus from an unfertilised egg, insert a nucleus from an adult body cell, give an electric shock, implant the embryo. Dolly the sheep.
cards.watch_out: In adult cell cloning, the clone is identical to the donor of the body cell nucleus, not the egg donor.
cards.grade9: Discuss issues, low variation, ethical concerns, low success rate, and possible benefits such as saving endangered species.

cards.title: Evidence for evolution and extinction
cards.question: What evidence supports evolution, and what causes extinction?
points: Fossils are remains of organisms from millions of years ago, from parts that did not decay, mineral replacement, or traces such as footprints.
The fossil record has gaps, as early life was soft-bodied and geological activity destroyed many fossils.
Antibiotic resistance evolves quickly because bacteria reproduce rapidly. MRSA is an example.
Extinction causes: new predators, new diseases, more successful competitors, catastrophic events, environmental change.
cards.watch_out: Bacteria are not immune. A chance mutation for resistance is selected.
cards.grade9: For antibiotic resistance, explain why finishing the course and limiting prescriptions slows it down.

cards.title: Classification and evolutionary trees
cards.question: How are living things classified, and what did Woese change?
points: Linnaeus: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
Binomial name: genus then species, for example Homo sapiens.
Woese used chemical analysis to propose three domains: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukaryota.
Evolutionary trees show how closely related organisms are, using current and fossil data.
cards.watch_out: The genus has a capital letter, the species does not.
cards.grade9: Explain that new evidence from microscopes and DNA analysis changed classification models. Science changes with evidence.

written.q: Describe how a starch-rich meal is digested and absorbed.
model: Teeth break food into smaller pieces, increasing surface area (1)
Salivary amylase begins breaking starch into sugars in the mouth (1)
Pancreatic amylase continues starch digestion in the small intestine (1)
Bile neutralises stomach acid, giving the right pH for enzymes (1)
Sugars (glucose) are absorbed through the villi of the small intestine (1)
By diffusion and active transport into the blood capillaries (1)

written.q: Explain how deforestation and the destruction of peat bogs affect biodiversity and global warming.
model: Deforestation removes habitats, reducing biodiversity (1)
Fewer trees means less CO₂ is absorbed by photosynthesis (1)
Burning and decay of wood releases CO₂ (1)
Peat bogs are destroyed to make compost, removing habitats (1)
Peat decays or burns, releasing CO₂ (1)
More CO₂ increases global warming, which changes species distribution and further reduces biodiversity (1)
Both are caused by uncontrolled cell division (1)
Benign tumours stay in one place, often in a membrane (1)
Malignant tumours invade tissues and spread in the blood to form secondary tumours (1)

written.q: Describe how to investigate the effect of different salt concentrations on the mass of potato tissue (required practical).
model: Cut potato cylinders of equal size with a cork borer and blot dry (1)
Measure and record the initial mass of each (1)
Place each in a different salt concentration, including 0 (distilled water) (1)
Keep time and temperature the same, for example 30 minutes at room temperature (1)
Remove, blot dry and reweigh; calculate percentage change in mass (1)
Repeat and calculate a mean; plot percentage change against concentration to find where there is no change (1)

written.q: A cell image is 8 mm long under a microscope. The magnification is × 400. Calculate the real length in micrometres and give your answer in standard form in metres.
model: Real size = image ÷ magnification (1)

written.q: Evaluate the use of embryonic stem cells to treat diseases such as type 1 diabetes. Give a conclusion.
model: Embryonic stem cells can differentiate into almost any cell, such as insulin-producing cells (1)
Could cure conditions rather than just treat symptoms (1)
Therapeutic cloning means cells have the patient's genes, so no rejection (1)
Ethical or religious objections to using and destroying embryos (1)
Risk of transferring viral infection, or cells could become cancerous (1)
Justified conclusion weighing benefits against risks (1)

written.q: Explain why root hair cells take in mineral ions by active transport and not by diffusion.
model: Mineral ion concentration in soil is lower than in the root hair cell (1)
So ions must move against the concentration gradient (1)
This needs energy from respiration, so active transport is used (1)

written.q: Describe how you would investigate the effect of pH on the rate of reaction of amylase.
model: Put iodine drops in a spotting tile (1)
Mix amylase, starch and a buffer of one pH in a water bath at a set temperature (1)
Every 10 seconds put a drop of the mixture onto fresh iodine (1)
Record the time when iodine stays orange-brown (starch gone) (1)
Repeat with buffers of different pH, keeping volumes and concentrations the same (1)
Calculate rate as 1 ÷ time and find the optimum pH (1)

written.q: Explain how the structure of an artery is related to its function.
model: Arteries carry blood at high pressure away from the heart (1)
Thick muscular walls withstand high pressure (1)
Elastic fibres stretch and recoil to keep blood flowing (1)
Narrow lumen maintains pressure (1)

written.q: Compare the use of stents and statins to treat coronary heart disease.
model: Stents are inserted to keep coronary arteries open (1)
Statins lower blood cholesterol and slow fatty build-up (1)
Stents act quickly, statins take time and must be taken long term (1)
Stents need surgery with a risk of infection or blood clots (1)
Statins can have side effects such as muscle pain or liver problems (1)
Comparison linked to patient situation, for example severity of the blockage (1)

written.q: Explain why the rate of transpiration increases on a hot, windy day.
model: Higher temperature gives water molecules more kinetic energy (1)
Faster evaporation and diffusion of water vapour from the leaf (1)
Wind removes water vapour from around the leaf (1)
This keeps the concentration gradient steep so diffusion out of stomata is faster (1)

written.q: Explain how bacteria become resistant to antibiotics.
model: Bacteria show variation; a random mutation gives resistance to an antibiotic (1)
When the antibiotic is used, non-resistant bacteria are killed (1)
Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce (1)
The resistance allele is passed on (1)
The resistant population grows quickly because bacteria reproduce rapidly (1)
Over time the whole population is resistant, for example MRSA (1)

written.q: Two parents are both heterozygous for brown eyes (Bb). Brown is dominant to blue. Use a Punnett square to find the probability of a blue-eyed child.
model: Gametes B and b from each parent (1)
Offspring BB, Bb, Bb, bb (1)
Only bb is blue-eyed (1)
Probability 1 in 4, 0.25 or 25% (1)

written.q: Describe how Dolly the sheep was produced by adult cell cloning, and give one issue with the technique.
model: Nucleus removed from an unfertilised egg cell (1)
Nucleus from an adult body cell of the sheep to be cloned is inserted (1)
Electric shock stimulates the egg to divide (1)
The embryo is implanted into the uterus of a host mother (1)
The offspring is genetically identical to the adult that gave the nucleus (1)
Issue such as low success rate, reduced variation, or ethical concerns (1)

written.q: Explain how a new species of finch could evolve on an isolated island.
model: A population becomes geographically isolated from the mainland (1)
Different conditions, such as food, act on the island population (1)
Natural selection favours different alleles in each population over many generations (1)
Eventually they cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring, so are separate species (1)

exam_tips.timing: Section A is 45 questions across all three sciences, so under a minute each. Leave time for Section B.
section_a: Read the command word first. State, describe, explain, compare, evaluate and calculate each want something different.
For multiple choice, cover the options and answer first, then find it.
In calculations, write the equation, substitute, convert units, then give the answer with units and sensible significant figures.
For required practical questions, name the independent, dependent and control variables.
section_b: 6 mark questions are marked by level. A clear, logical sequence of points scores Level 3 (5 to 6 marks).
Explain means give a reason using because, so or which means.
Evaluate means give pros, cons and a justified conclusion.
Compare means give similarities and differences, using whereas in each point.
grade9: Use precise keywords from the AQA specification, such as partially permeable membrane and denatured.
Define fully. A tissue is a group of cells with a similar structure and function, not just cells working together.
Name the structure, then explain how it helps the function. Thick elastic artery walls withstand high pressure and stretch and recoil.
Chain your reasoning with no jumps. Less oxygen, less aerobic respiration, less energy released.
In practical questions name the independent variable, the dependent variable and the controls. More repeats do not fix a weak method.
Use data in your answer. Quote numbers from graphs and tables, and process them (difference, percentage change).
week: Most days, 10 to 15 minutes: press Start today (due cards, the new batch, then a short quiz).
Once a week, 15 minutes: one 4 to 6 mark Written practice question, about a minute a mark, then mark it point by point. Each point needs a because.
Once a week: a quiz on the Quiz tab that mixes older units with this week's, so earlier topics stay in.
Fix one mistake: rewrite one wrong answer or one watch out from memory, then check it against the card.

mcq.q: Lactase digests lactose fastest at pH 8. Why is it unlikely to be made in the stomach?
mcq.a: The stomach is acidic, but lactase works best in neutral or alkaline conditions
w: Lactose is not found in the stomach
mcq.e: Low pH in the stomach would slow or denature lactase.

mcq.q: Cyanide stops respiration. Glucose absorption falls when cyanide is added. What does this show?
mcq.a: Glucose is absorbed partly by active transport, which needs energy
w: Glucose is absorbed only by diffusion
Glucose is not absorbed at all
mcq.e: Active transport uses energy from respiration.

mcq.q: Xylose is absorbed at the same rate with or without cyanide. How is it absorbed?
mcq.e: Diffusion does not need energy from respiration.

mcq.q: Why does the pH fall when lipase digests fat in milk?
mcq.e: Fat is broken into fatty acids and glycerol.

mcq.q: Why do the cells lining the small intestine have many mitochondria?
mcq.a: To release energy for active transport
mcq.e: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration.

mcq.q: Which organs produce amylase?
mcq.a: Salivary glands, pancreas and small intestine
mcq.e: Amylase is made in three places.

mcq.q: Why must biological washing powder be used below 45 °C?
w: Enzymes only work in cold water
Stains are removed by heat anyway
mcq.e: The active site changes shape above the optimum.

mcq.q: The pH falls from 8.7 to 7.7 between 4 and 8 minutes. What is the average rate of fall?
Oxygen uptake by the intestine rises by 50% when glucose is present. What does this suggest?
mcq.a: More respiration is releasing energy to absorb glucose by active transport
mcq.e: Active transport needs energy from aerobic respiration.

mcq.q: Which feature is found in a prokaryotic cell but not an animal cell?
mcq.e: Bacteria often have small rings of DNA called plasmids.

mcq.q: Where is the genetic material of a bacterium?
mcq.a: A single loop in the cytoplasm
mcq.e: Prokaryotes have no nucleus.

mcq.q: Which structure synthesises proteins?
mcq.e: Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis.

mcq.q: What is the cell wall of a plant cell made of?
mcq.e: Plant cell walls are cellulose.

mcq.q: Why do muscle cells have many mitochondria?
mcq.e: Aerobic respiration in mitochondria transfers energy.

mcq.q: What is differentiation?
mcq.e: Cells gain the structures for a particular function.

mcq.q: An image is 15 mm long and the real cell is 30 µm. What is the magnification?
Why can an electron microscope see ribosomes when a light microscope cannot?
mcq.e: Resolution is the ability to distinguish two close points.

mcq.q: How many micrometres are in 1 mm?
Why are agar plates incubated at 25 °C in schools?
mcq.a: To reduce the growth of human pathogens
w: To speed up growth to the maximum
To stop the agar melting only
mcq.e: Lower temperature slows pathogens that grow at body temperature.

mcq.q: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. How many bacteria come from one cell after 2 hours?
mcq.e: 2 hours = 6 divisions, 2⁶ = 64.

mcq.q: A clear zone has a radius of 5 mm. What is its area (π = 3.14)?
Why is the inoculating loop passed through a flame?
mcq.a: To kill unwanted microorganisms on it
mcq.e: This is part of aseptic technique.

mcq.q: What happens in the first stage of the cell cycle?
mcq.a: The cell grows and copies its DNA
mcq.e: DNA replication happens before mitosis.

mcq.q: Mitosis produces
w: Two cells with half the chromosomes
mcq.e: Mitosis is for growth and repair.

mcq.q: Where are stem cells found in plants?
mcq.e: Meristems are at root and shoot tips.

mcq.q: Why are cells from therapeutic cloning not rejected?
mcq.a: They have the same genes as the patient
mcq.e: The embryo is made with the patient's genetic material.

mcq.q: Which is a risk of using stem cells?
mcq.e: Contaminated stem cells could pass on viruses.

mcq.q: What is osmosis?
mcq.a: Diffusion of water through a partially permeable membrane
w: Movement of any particle against a gradient
mcq.e: Water moves from dilute to concentrated solution.

mcq.q: A potato cylinder goes from 4.00 g to 4.40 g. What is the percentage change in mass?
Why are potato cylinders blotted dry before weighing?
mcq.a: To remove surface solution that adds mass
mcq.e: Only water inside the tissue should count.

mcq.q: How do root hair cells absorb mineral ions?
mcq.e: Ions are more concentrated in the root than the soil.

mcq.q: What does active transport need that diffusion does not?
mcq.e: Moving against the gradient needs energy.

mcq.q: What is the surface area to volume ratio of a cube with 3 cm sides?
mcq.e: SA 54 cm², volume 27 cm³.

mcq.q: Why do large animals need specialised exchange surfaces?
mcq.a: Their surface area to volume ratio is small
w: They have more cells that need no oxygen
mcq.e: Diffusion across the outside is too slow.

mcq.q: Which is the correct order of organisation?
mcq.e: Each level builds on the one before.

mcq.q: What are the products of lipid digestion?
mcq.e: Lipase breaks lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.

mcq.q: Where is protease made?
mcq.e: Pepsin is a stomach protease.

mcq.q: What is the lock and key model?
mcq.a: The substrate fits the active site of a specific enzyme
w: Enzymes are used up in reactions
mcq.e: Shape determines specificity.

mcq.q: What happens to an enzyme above its optimum temperature?
mcq.a: The active site changes shape and it is denatured
mcq.e: Bonds holding the shape break.

mcq.q: In the amylase practical starch has gone after 40 s. What is the rate?
mcq.e: rate = 1 ÷ 40.

mcq.q: Which reagent tests for protein?
mcq.e: Biuret turns purple with protein.

mcq.q: Which food test needs heating?
mcq.e: Benedict's needs a hot water bath.

mcq.q: Where is bile made?
mcq.e: Bile is stored in the gall bladder but made in the liver.

mcq.q: How does bile speed up fat digestion?
mcq.a: It emulsifies fat, increasing surface area
w: It is an enzyme that breaks bonds
It makes the small intestine acidic
It absorbs fat into the blood
mcq.e: Smaller droplets give lipase more surface.

mcq.q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the heart to the lungs?
mcq.e: It carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart.

mcq.q: Why is the left ventricle wall thicker than the right?
mcq.a: It pumps blood all round the body at higher pressure
w: It receives blood from the lungs
mcq.e: The body circuit needs more pressure.

mcq.q: Where is the natural pacemaker?
mcq.e: Pacemaker cells set the resting heart rate.

mcq.q: Which blood vessels have valves?
mcq.e: Valves prevent backflow at low pressure.

mcq.q: Why do red blood cells have no nucleus?
mcq.e: More haemoglobin carries more oxygen.

mcq.q: What are platelets?
mcq.a: Cell fragments that help blood clot
mcq.e: They have no nucleus.

mcq.q: 1500 ml of blood passes through a vessel in 2.5 minutes. What is the rate?
Which treatment lowers blood cholesterol?
mcq.e: Statins slow fatty build-up.

mcq.q: A disadvantage of a mechanical heart valve is
mcq.a: The patient must take anti-clotting drugs
w: It wears out in a few months
mcq.e: Clots can form on mechanical valves.

mcq.q: What makes a tumour malignant?
mcq.a: It invades tissue and spreads in the blood
w: It is caused by a virus only
It is made of dead cells
mcq.e: Malignant tumours form secondary tumours.

mcq.q: Which is a non-communicable disease?
mcq.e: Non-communicable diseases are not caused by pathogens.

mcq.q: Which leaf tissue contains the most chloroplasts?
mcq.e: It is near the top surface for light.

mcq.q: What controls the opening of stomata?
mcq.e: Guard cells change shape to open and close stomata.

mcq.q: What does phloem transport?
mcq.e: This is translocation.

mcq.q: Which condition increases the rate of transpiration?
mcq.e: Wind removes water vapour and keeps the gradient steep.

mcq.q: A potometer bubble moves 45 mm in 9 minutes. What is the rate?
How many gametes does one cell make in meiosis?
mcq.e: The cell divides twice.

mcq.q: Which is an advantage of asexual reproduction?
mcq.e: Asexual reproduction is fast and needs no mate.

mcq.q: Which organism reproduces both sexually and asexually?
mcq.e: Strawberries use runners and seeds.

mcq.q: What is a gene?
mcq.a: A small section of DNA that codes for a protein
mcq.e: Genes code for a sequence of amino acids.

mcq.q: Which base pairs with adenine in DNA?
mcq.e: A pairs with T, C pairs with G.

mcq.q: How many bases code for one amino acid?
mcq.e: A triplet codes for one amino acid.

mcq.q: A nucleotide is made of
mcq.a: A sugar, a phosphate and a base
w: An amino acid and a sugar
mcq.e: DNA is a polymer of nucleotides.

mcq.q: What is a heterozygous genotype?
mcq.a: Two different alleles, such as Bb
mcq.e: Hetero means different.

mcq.q: Two carriers of cystic fibrosis (Ff × Ff) have a child. What is the chance it has cystic fibrosis?
mcq.e: Only ff of the four boxes is affected.

mcq.q: Polydactyly is caused by
mcq.e: One copy is enough.

mcq.q: What are the sex chromosomes of a male?
mcq.e: Females are XX.

mcq.q: Why was Mendel's work not accepted in his lifetime?
mcq.a: Genes and chromosomes had not been discovered
mcq.e: There was no mechanism to explain his results.

mcq.q: What is a mutation?
mcq.a: A change in the DNA base sequence
w: A change caused only by the environment
mcq.e: Mutations create new alleles.

mcq.q: Which characteristic is caused by both genes and environment?
mcq.e: Genes set potential, diet affects actual height.

mcq.q: In natural selection, which individuals are most likely to reproduce?
mcq.a: Those best suited to the environment
mcq.e: They survive to pass on alleles.

mcq.q: Two populations are different species when they
mcq.a: Cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring
mcq.e: Fertile offspring is the test.

mcq.q: Who independently proposed natural selection alongside Darwin?
mcq.e: Wallace also studied warning colouration.

mcq.q: A risk of selective breeding is
mcq.e: Low variation increases disease risk.

mcq.q: In genetic engineering, what is used to cut out the gene?
mcq.e: Restriction enzymes cut DNA.

mcq.q: What is a vector in genetic engineering?
mcq.a: A plasmid or virus that carries the gene into cells
w: The organism that gives the gene
mcq.e: Vectors deliver the gene.

mcq.q: In adult cell cloning, what is removed from the unfertilised egg?
mcq.e: The donor nucleus replaces it.

mcq.q: Which cloning method splits an early embryo?
mcq.e: The parts are implanted into host mothers.

mcq.q: Why does antibiotic resistance evolve quickly in bacteria?
mcq.e: Many generations pass in a short time.

mcq.q: Which is a reason for gaps in the fossil record?
mcq.e: Soft tissue rarely fossilises.

mcq.q: Which is the correct binomial name?
mcq.e: Genus capital, species lower case.

mcq.q: What did Carl Woese propose?
mcq.a: Three domains: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukaryota
mcq.e: Based on chemical analysis.

mcq.q: Which organ makes bile?
mcq.e: Bile is stored in the gall bladder.

mcq.q: Why does the stomach produce hydrochloric acid?
mcq.a: To kill bacteria and give the right pH for protease
mcq.e: Stomach protease works best in acid.

mcq.q: Where are the products of digestion absorbed into the blood?
mcq.e: Villi give a large surface area.

mcq.q: What does the large intestine mainly absorb?
mcq.e: Most nutrients are absorbed earlier.

mcq.q: Which feature of a villus speeds up absorption?
mcq.a: A single layer of surface cells
mcq.e: A short diffusion distance.

mcq.q: What is a malignant tumour?
mcq.a: A tumour that invades tissues and spreads in the blood
w: A tumour that stays in one place
A tumour caused only by viruses
mcq.e: Malignant tumours form secondary tumours.

mcq.q: Cancer is caused by
mcq.e: Cells divide by mitosis without control.

mcq.q: What is biodiversity?
mcq.a: The variety of different species in an ecosystem or on Earth
w: The number of individuals of one species
The total mass of living things
mcq.e: More species means more stability.

mcq.q: Why is high biodiversity good for an ecosystem?
mcq.a: It makes the ecosystem more stable
mcq.e: Species depend less on any one other species.

mcq.q: Which pollutes water?
mcq.e: Fertiliser washes into rivers.

mcq.q: Why is destroying peat bogs harmful?
mcq.a: It releases carbon dioxide and destroys habitats
mcq.e: Peat is a carbon store.

mcq.q: Which is a reason for tropical deforestation?
mcq.e: Also cattle and rice.

mcq.q: How does deforestation increase atmospheric carbon dioxide?
mcq.a: Less photosynthesis and burning of trees
mcq.e: Fewer trees absorb CO₂.

mcq.q: Which is a biological consequence of global warming?
mcq.a: Changes in the distribution of species
mcq.e: Species move as climate changes.

mcq.q: Which helps maintain biodiversity on farms?
mcq.e: Hedgerows provide habitats.

mcq.q: Which two greenhouse gases are increasing in the atmosphere and causing global warming?
mcq.e: Their levels are rising.

vocab.meaning: To make a process easier or faster
vocab.example: Bile facilitates the digestion of fats by emulsifying them.

vocab.meaning: To make something bad less severe
vocab.example: Statins mitigate the risk of a heart attack.
Cancer cells proliferate without control.
Some mutations have deleterious effects on proteins.
Bacteria are ubiquitous in soil, water and air.

vocab.meaning: To speed up a reaction without being used up
vocab.example: Amylase catalyses the breakdown of starch.

vocab.meaning: To change a protein's shape so it no longer works
vocab.example: High temperatures denature enzymes.

vocab.meaning: Adapted to carry out a particular function
vocab.example: Sperm cells are specialised for swimming.
The cell membrane is partially permeable.

vocab.meaning: The amount of a substance in a given volume
vocab.example: Oxygen moves down its concentration gradient.
A correlation does not prove one causes the other.
Mendel tested his hypothesis using pea plants.
Darwin gathered empirical evidence on his voyage.

vocab.meaning: To check or prove that something is correct
vocab.example: Peer review helps validate new findings.
Ignore anomalous results when calculating a mean.

vocab.meaning: Existing as a natural, permanent part
vocab.example: Variation is inherent in sexual reproduction.

vocab.meaning: Likely to be affected or harmed
vocab.example: Inbred animals are more susceptible to disease.
The resistant allele became predominant in the population.
The ratio diminishes as the organism gets larger.
Villi augment the surface area of the small intestine.
The active site changes shape; consequently, the substrate no longer fits.

vocab.meaning: In addition, used to add a point
vocab.example: Furthermore, GM crops can increase yields.
Arteries have thick walls; conversely, veins have thin walls.
Stents work quickly, albeit with a risk of clots.
Scientists scrutinise data before publishing.

vocab.meaning: Open to more than one meaning
vocab.example: An ambiguous conclusion loses marks.

vocab.meaning: To provide evidence that something is true
vocab.example: Fossils substantiate the theory of evolution.

vocab.meaning: To say something is caused by something else
vocab.example: The rise in disease can be attributed to inbreeding.

vocab.meaning: To extend a pattern beyond the measured data
vocab.example: Extrapolate the line to estimate the rate at 60 °C.
Homeostasis keeps body temperature near 37 °C.
Isolated populations can form new species.
DNA replicates before a cell divides.
A rigorous method controls all other variables.
Not all cloned embryos are viable.
We can infer that the enzyme was denatured.
